title: Without end
hook: God as the Infinite, beyond any description

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Creation, where the letters are engraved, weighed and combined. Your line was letters create. Did one sentence of yours get read back slowly? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

How do you draw something with no edges? Every drawing starts with a line, and a line is a boundary: this is inside, that is outside. A word works the same way. Call something kind, and you've drawn a line around it, kind and not cruel. Call it great, and you've measured it against something smaller. Now try it with God. Every word you reach for draws a line. Wise. Strong. Near. Each one is true in its way, and each one is too small. Jewish mystics gave a name to that problem, a name that is really a refusal to draw any line at all. Today's word.
screen: `EVERY DRAWING STARTS WITH A LINE.` → `EVERY WORD DRAWS A BOUNDARY.` → `EACH ONE IS TOO SMALL.`

segments.voice: Ein Sof. In Hebrew, ein means there is no, and sof means end. Without end. Kabbalists use it for God as God is in God's own self, before and beyond any way of being known. Turn it four ways. First, it is hardly a name. A name usually tells you what something is. This one tells you only what it is not: not ending, not bounded, not measured. Readers who spent the last weeks with Maimonides will hear a cousin of his teaching, that we speak more truly of God by saying what God is not. The kabbalists take that silence and give it a title. Second, the Psalms point the same way. The psalmist praises God and then admits that God's greatness is beyond searching out. Praise, and then the edge of what praise can do. Third, Ein Sof is not a second God hiding behind the first. Kabbalists are insistent that God is one. Ein Sof is how they speak of the one God from the side that can't be spoken of: not a different being, but the same One, seen from where every word runs out. Fourth, and here's the turn. If God is without end, beyond every description, how does God touch a world with edges, a world of kitchens and buses and birthdays? That question drives the whole system you're about to meet. The mystics answer it with lights. For today, just stand where they stood, at the edge of the drawing, looking at the space with no line around it.
screen: `THERE IS NO END.` · `A NAME THAT SAYS WHAT GOD IS NOT.` · `NOT A SECOND GOD.` · `HOW DOES THE ENDLESS TOUCH THE WORLD?` · then, large: `WITHOUT END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the open sky. If you can, step outside or go to a window. If you can't, close your eyes and remember the widest sky you've ever seen. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes go up, past the roofs and the wires and the trees, to where there's nothing to rest on. Notice how your gaze wants to find an edge, a cloud, a bird, and let it keep going instead. You don't have to name anything. If you pray, you can simply be quiet before the One without end. The bell holds the time.
Ein Sof. Without end: the kabbalists' way of speaking of God as God is in God's self, beyond every name and description. Today's word.
Your line: without end. Today, whenever you catch the sky out of the corner of your eye, let that be your reminder of the space with no line around it. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: In Kabbalah, Ein Sof is the term for God beyond all description; students usually meet it at the start of an introduction to the sefirot, as the one source from which everything else unfolds.

myth: Ein Sof is a second God behind the God of the Torah
kabbalists insist God is one. Ein Sof speaks of the one God from the side that can't be described.
the name Ein Sof says what God is not
not ending, not bounded: a name built from a refusal to draw a line.
kabbalists say Ein Sof can be fully described with the right words
the whole point of the name is that every description is too small.

fork.setup: you've just said God is without end, beyond every description. a friend asks: then how does God touch a world of kitchens and buses?
options: God doesn't touch the world at all.
that's the question the mystics answer next, with lights.
God must have edges after all.
fork.reveal: the kabbalists' whole system grows from this question. their answer comes as lights, the sefirot.

original.note: Hebrew: there is no end. The kabbalists' term for God beyond all description.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mystical nickname for God.
what it means: a name that says only what God is not, not ending, not bounded, for God beyond every description.
what a scholar hears: a kin of the teaching that God is best spoken of by what God is not, set at the head of the kabbalists' picture of how the one God relates to the world.

notes: Maimonides' negative attributes (Guide 1:58) are mentioned only as a 'cousin' of the Ein Sof idea, without claiming historical influence; please confirm the framing.
'Some teachers say that from Ein Sof's side, nothing can even be described as revealed' is a general paraphrase of kabbalistic teaching; please confirm or cut.
History of the term (early kabbalists in Provence and Gerona) deliberately left out under the claims rule.
Editor: replaced the garbled, unsourced line 'from Ein Sof's side, nothing can even be described as revealed' with a plain restatement of the one-God point.
